newsitem.title: USA: Existing home sales down in September.
newsitem.headline: Existing home sales down in September.

text.p: Sales of existing homes fell for the fourth consecutive month in September, as consumers scaled back home buying in response to higher interest rates, the National Association of Realtors said Friday.
Despite the decline, the underlying trend in housing remained relatively strong, the real estate group said.

Sales of existing, or previously owned, homes fell 2.9 percent in September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.02 million, it said. That followed a revised decline of 0.2 percent to a rate of 4.14 million in August.
The real estate agents' group said the figures reflected caution among consumers because of higher interest rates.

The average rate for a 30-year mortgage loan in September was 8.23 percent, up from 8.0 percent in August and near July's average rate of 8.25 percent, according to the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp., or Freddie Mac.
Still, while September resales declined, the rate of existing home sales remained above 4 million, a sign of underlying strength in the housing sector.
"The market is very healthy and we expect sales to remain firm through the remainder of the year," said Art Godi, president of the National Association of Realtors.

The group raised its estimate of August sales to an annual rate of 4.14 million from the 4.13 million previously reported. Sales of existing homes peaked in May at a record rate of 4.28 million a year.
The group's chief economist, John Tuccillo, predicted that mortgage rates probably have peaked for the year and will begin to drift down through the rest of 1996.
Freddie Mac said Thursday that 30-year mortgages averaged 7.86 percent this week, down from 7.88 percent last week. Fifteen-year loans dipped to 7.37 percent from 7.39 percent.

"Consumers will most likely sit tight and wait for those drops," Tuccillo said. He said he expects 30-year, fixed-rate mortgages to register a larger drop than rates on one-year adjustable-rate loans.
The decline in September existing homes sales was sharper than forecast by Wall Street economists, who had expected a drop in the sales rate to 4.11 million a year.
The average price for an existing home sold in September fell to $117,700 from $122,300 in August.
Sales in the Northeast rose 5.3 percent. In the South, the nation's biggest housing market, sales fell 3.7 percent.
In the Midwest, sales edged up 0.7 percent and in the West they fell 13.4 percent.
